editorialPurpose: Understand motor-related prediction and weaker self-touch, while distinguishing light ticklishness from incompletely explained tickle laughter.
storyAngle: Motor prediction helps explain weaker self-touch, while the laughter question remains incompletely solved.

segments.text: Why can their fingers make you laugh, but yours usually can't?
Both touch your skin. One important clue is prediction.
When you move your hand, your nervous system can anticipate the touch it will produce.
That touch can feel weaker. Scientists call this sensory attenuation.
In experiments, self-produced touch felt less ticklish than matching external touch.
Adding a delay to a robotic self-touch made it feel more ticklish.
But those experiments used light touch, not full-on tickle laughter.
You can give yourself a light, tickly sensation. Laughter-inducing tickling is harder to explain, and people differ.
Prediction is an important clue, not the whole answer.
Your nervous system doesn't just receive touch. It can anticipate your own.

narrativeStructure.label: Their hand. Your hand.
narrativeStructure.purpose: Immediate macro of external fingers touching ribs, sculpted faceless person recoils; match into visibly connected self-hand with much smaller reaction. No laughter recording or clinical demonstration.

narrativeStructure.label: Touch remains
narrativeStructure.purpose: Two same-material skin surfaces indent under touch; keep sensation motif visible in both; no absence of sensory input.

narrativeStructure.label: Movement has consequences
narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera opens from the self-hand into an abstract prediction model: intended movement branches to anticipated contact and hand action, then actual tactile feedback enters. Conceptual model, not anatomical pathway.

narrativeStructure.label: Reduced, not erased
narrativeStructure.purpose: Expected and actual contact motifs align, then a smaller but nonzero felt-touch motif emerges. Illustrative magnitude only, no calibrated neural signal.

narrativeStructure.label: Matched touch
narrativeStructure.purpose: Same original palm and soft probe; self-produced and external condition shown in matched scale with different subjective sensation motifs. No laughter implied.

narrativeStructure.label: Delay breaks the match
narrativeStructure.purpose: Original simplified robot control and forearm probe: hand moves a stylus first, probe follows later; expected and actual contact motifs separate in time. Motion expanded, no exact apparatus reproduction.

narrativeStructure.label: The crucial distinction
narrativeStructure.purpose: Pull back from robot light touch to same person at ribs, side-by-side light brushing and stronger tickle; no transition suggesting measured laughter from robot.

narrativeStructure.label: Different experiences
narrativeStructure.purpose: A light self-brush remains visibly felt; three sculpted figures show different external tickle reactions. Individual/context differences illustrated, not study-derived categories.

narrativeStructure.label: An incomplete explanation
narrativeStructure.purpose: Return to self and external contrast, show prediction as one contributing strand with open space instead of a complete circuit. No claim social anticipation alone explains laughter.

narrativeStructure.label: See it coming
narrativeStructure.purpose: Return to original self-hand; translucent anticipated contact precedes physical arrival, actual touch persists. One concise illustrated reframe with no CTA.
